channel.title: The Dig — HPC-QC integration and resource management
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the HPC-QC integration and resource management preset. Today’s ranked reading list collects six relevance-3 skims that sit around the edges of neutral-atom and spin-qubit control, QEC, and HPC integration: 2611.17652 on an FPGA-based quantum data processing unit, 2611.17262 on scalable Pauli propagation, 2611.16971 on benchmarked-noise zero-noise extrapolation, 2611.18378 on structure and trainability in quantum circuits, 2611.16285 on multi-GPU orchestration for relay belief-propagation decoding, and 2611.16271 on hierarchical QEC decoding. Together they are useful for transferable methods and infrastructure context rather than direct spin-qubit operation, calibration, or benchmarking. No pay dirt today — 3 to skim.

item.title: Quantum Data Processing Unit for Neutral-Atom Quantum Computers
item.description:
Skim new method — FPGA-based QDPU architecture classifies a 50×50 atom array in 12.5 μs using one matched-filter lane. Eliminating an assumed 150 ms host round trip increases simulated 35×35 target assembly success from 8% to 85% and cuts wall-clock time per assembly from 19 s to 0.16 s.

Grade 0.556 · 4.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Accelerating HPC With Quantum Computing: It Is a Software Challenge Too” · Pranav Srinivas Murali, Russell Marroquin Solares, Warren Zhou, Wanda Hou, Anil Bilgin, Yi-Zhuang You

Figure

Target assembly success plotted against added per-cycle host round-trip latency across multiple trap lifetimes, showing severe fidelity degradation when host communications add tens of milliseconds.

Asks

How can classical measurement processing and rearrangement feedback be architected to meet tight real-time latency budgets in scaling neutral-atom quantum processors?

But

Simulated atom-loss model assumes 60 s trap lifetime and 0.1% loss per moved atom; CNN detector for 104 sites exceeds DSP limits on the target device.

Tools

AMD Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC (xczu49dr on ZCU216) · NVIDIA DGX Spark over 10 GbE NVQLink · Matched-filter and CNN detection pipelines · Quantised GraphMP ranking kernel

Abstract

Quantum computers need real-time classical processing to convert measurement data into feedback within device-specific timing constraints. We introduce the quantum data processing unit (QDPU), an architecture between a quantum device and its controller. Its core is a machine-learned quantum data model (QDM), adapted to the measurement response and noise characteristics of the device. We implement an FPGA pipeline for neutral-atom array assembly that performs occupancy detection and rearrangement scheduling in FPGA logic. One calibrated matched-filter lane classifies a 50×50 array in 12.5 μs. An atom-loss model using a software reference planner evaluates a 35×35 target with a 60 s trap lifetime and 0.1% loss per moved atom. Removing an assumed 150 ms host round trip raises the predicted assembly success from 8% to 85% and reduces the wall-clock time per successful assembly from 19 s to 0.16 s. A GPU-based outer loop is proposed for refitting model parameters between runs. Its NVQLink transport is measured on the board: over 10 GbE to an NVIDIA DGX Spark, the median FPGA-to-host-to-FPGA round trip is 2.74 μs for 128-byte messages forwarded by a CPU core. A separate 12-bit learned qLDPC kernel is placed and routed for the same FPGA target, with a derived latency of 0.84 ms per round for a [[1122,148]] lifted-product code under code-capacity noise. A quantised GraphMP ranking kernel for the same code runs on the board with a median host-to-FPGA-to-host latency of 50.5 μs with one shot in flight, excluding host-side BP+OSD post-processing. Together, these implementations illustrate a shared architecture with workload-specific models and timing requirements.

item.title: Scalable Pauli propagation through F₂-linear partitioning
item.description:
Skim new method — Partitioning Pauli strings with an 𝔽2-linear hash restricts exchanges under any k-qubit channel to at most 4k predetermined partitions, enabling local deduplication and weak-scaling efficiencies of 68–74% across 32 compute nodes with up to 1.6×1011 Pauli strings.

Grade 0.521 · 4.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computers for High-Performance Computing”

Figure

Communication fraction fex, load imbalance λ, and wall time T plotted against worker count P for different node-hash strategies simulating a 127-qubit kicked Ising circuit.

Asks

How can the global communication and synchronization bottleneck during deduplication in parallel Pauli propagation be eliminated?

But

Trotterized dynamics simulations; load balance degrades when tailoring node hashes to avoid communication across many workers (P≫1).

Tools

binary symplectic representation · F₂-linear hash partitioning · MPI distributed computing · work-stealing scheduling

Code. https://github.com/lkdvos/paulistrings-rs

Abstract

Pauli propagation simulates quantum circuits and many-body dynamics by evolving observables in the Heisenberg picture as sparse sums of Pauli strings. As Pauli-string operations reduce to bit manipulations, its performance is limited by memory bandwidth and capacity rather than computational throughput. Pooling the memory of many cores and nodes is hindered by the deduplication step after every gate, which can require global synchronization. We avoid this bottleneck by partitioning the strings with an F₂-linear hash function, which guarantees that a k-qubit channel couples each partition to at most 4^k partitions fixed by the gate, decomposing gate application into independent tasks with bounded communication. Benchmarks of our open-source implementation demonstrate efficient parallel scaling within and across compute nodes, enabling simulations with over 10¹¹ Pauli strings and extending the accessible timescales of quantum many-body dynamics.

item.title: Scaling Pêlagos: Multi-GPU Orchestration for Relay Belief-Propagation Decoding
item.description:
Skim incremental — Process-isolated orchestration achieves eight-GPU end-to-end speedups of 5.68× (MI300X) and 6.23× (MI355X) on one-gross ([[144,12,12]]) circuits, and 6.92× and 7.01× on two-gross ([[288,12,18]]) circuits. Isolated GPU decoding time alone yields 7.58× and 7.45× speedups on the two-gross code.

Grade 0.507 · 3.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computers for High-Performance Computing”

Figure

End-to-end and GPU-only scaling speedup as a function of GPU count (1, 2, 4, 8) normalized to single-GPU throughput, comparing baseline multi-GPU Pêlagos to the process-isolated implementation across one-gross and two-gross codes.

Asks

How can host-side orchestration bottlenecks be eliminated to achieve near-linear multi-GPU scaling for Pêlagos relay belief-propagation decoding on single-node GPU clusters?

Before

Original Pêlagos used a single host Python process managing multiple HIP device contexts with serial preprocessing; the new design improves eight-GPU throughput over this baseline by >2× on one-gross, and by 1.48× (MI300X) and 1.36× (MI355X) on two-gross.

But

Fixed batch size of 1,024 syndromes per GPU; maximum batch bounded by signed 32-bit indexing (E×B≤231−1); circuit-level depolarizing noise at physical error rate p=0.003 and relay limit R=50.

Tools

Pêlagos Relay-BP decoder · AMD Instinct MI300X and MI355X GPUs · Process-isolated HIP contexts · Host shared-memory output collection · Bivariate bicycle codes

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum error-correction (QEC) decoders that achieve low logical error rates under real-time operating constraints. These constraints motivate heuristic decoding algorithms whose error-correction performance must be evaluated through large-scale simulation. High-throughput decoding accelerates this evaluation and the exploration of decoder parameters. Using multiple graphics processing units (GPUs) is a natural way to scale these simulations, but naively distributing syndrome batches introduces host-side preprocessing and output-collection overheads that limit scaling. To address these limitations, we extend the Pêlagos relay belief-propagation (Relay-BP) decoder with process-isolated orchestration, parallel host preprocessing, and shared-memory output. We evaluate both one-gross ([[144,12,12]]) and two-gross ([[288,12,18]]) codes in a multi-GPU environment. Specifically, for the one-gross circuit at R=50, eight AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and eight AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs achieve optimized end-to-end speedups of 5.68× and 6.23×, respectively. For the two-gross circuit, the corresponding speedups are 6.92× and 7.01×. When throughput is calculated using GPU decoding time, the corresponding two-gross speedups are 7.58× and 7.45×, indicating near-linear GPU scaling. We deploy Pêlagos on Lux, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's AMD Instinct MI355X-based supercomputer, as a pathfinding application for high-throughput QEC simulation. This deployment provides a concrete quantum-computing use case for the AI + HPC infrastructure supporting the Genesis Mission's scientific-discovery goals. These end-to-end measurements demonstrate a practical path to accelerating large-scale QEC simulation through efficient multi-GPU decoding.
